ddx.step1_summary:
- Chief complaint: Pain on urination (dysuria).
- Symptoms: Dysuria for 6 days; lower central abdominal (suprapubic) pain, intermittent, severity ~7/10; malodorous urine; visible blood in urine described as spots (hematuria); able to pass urine; no fever or feeling feverish; no loin/flank pain; no vaginal discharge; no change in appetite or bowel habit; first episode.
- Past medical history: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) only; no prior UTIs reported.
- Medications / Allergies: Mebeverine 200 mg three times daily; allergy to clindamycin.
- Family / Social history: Lives with friends; works as a support worker; drinks occasionally (≈1 glass wine/week); non-smoker; no family medical problems reported.
- Vital signs / exam findings: None documented in transcript (physician asked patient to check temperature at home; no temperature recorded).
- Labs / Imaging: None performed or documented during this visit.

V: Urolithiasis (urinary tract stone): Hematuria and intermittent (colicky) lower abdominal pain can be caused by urinary stones; stones can also irritate the bladder/urethra causing dysuria.
I: Acute uncomplicated cystitis (lower UTI): Dysuria, suprapubic pain, malodorous urine and hematuria in a female are classic for bladder infection.
Urethritis (including sexually transmitted infections such as Chlamydia or Gonorrhea): Can present with dysuria and sometimes urethral bleeding or spotting; may have minimal vaginal discharge.

Acute pyelonephritis: Ascending infection causing urinary symptoms plus systemic features (fever, flank pain) — less likely here because fever and flank pain absent but still a consideration if symptoms progress.
N: Bladder (urothelial) cancer: Painless hematuria is the common presentation; should be considered in any patient with visible hematuria, though less likely in younger patients without risk factors.
D: Interstitial cystitis / painful bladder syndrome: Chronic bladder pain and dysuria without infection; usually a chronic condition rather than a new 6-day episode, but can present with suprapubic pain and urinary symptoms.
I2: Iatrogenic causes (recent instrumentation/catheterisation or drug-induced hemorrhagic cystitis): Can cause hematuria and dysuria — no history of instrumentation or known offending drugs in transcript, so unlikely but part of differential.
C: Congenital urinary tract anomaly (eg vesicoureteral reflux or structural abnormality): Could predispose to haematuria or recurrent UTIs, but patient reports first episode and no known history — unlikely as an acute explanation.
A: Autoimmune / glomerular disease (eg IgA nephropathy, SLE-related nephritis): Can cause hematuria; typically associated with other systemic signs (edema, hypertension, proteinuria) which are not reported — less likely for isolated dysuria and suprapubic pain.
T: Traumatic urethral/bladder injury: Recent trauma or sexual injury can cause hematuria and dysuria — patient denies trauma; unlikely.
E: Endocrine / metabolic predisposition to infection (eg diabetes mellitus): Diabetes increases UTI risk; no history or features of diabetes reported, but metabolic causes that predispose to infection are a background consideration.

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Acute uncomplicated cystitis (lower urinary tract infection)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Female with 6 days of dysuria, suprapubic pain, malodorous urine and visible haematuria — classic presentation for an uncomplicated bladder infection. No fever or flank pain suggesting lower tract rather than upper tract involvement.
supporting_evidence: Visible spotting of blood in urine
Female sex and no systemic features (consistent with uncomplicated cystitis)
opposing_evidence: No documented urinary frequency or urgency explicitly mentioned (but not required)
No urine dip/culture or imaging to confirm infection
No prior UTIs (first episode) — not opposing but limits chronic diagnoses

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Urethritis / Sexually transmitted infection (e.g., Chlamydia, Gonorrhea)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Urethritis can present with dysuria and bleeding/spotting from the urethra and may have little or no discharge. Sexual history in the visit was limited/negative for regular intercourse but not fully explored; STI should be considered especially if symptoms persist despite empiric UTI therapy.
supporting_evidence: Absence of overt vaginal discharge does not exclude urethritis
opposing_evidence: Patient denied recent sexual activity when asked (though history may be incomplete)
No purulent urethral or vaginal discharge reported
STI risk factors not elicited (no new partners documented)

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Intermittent (colicky) lower abdominal pain and hematuria are compatible with urinary tract stones; stones can also cause dysuria if they irritate the bladder/urethra. Lack of flank/loin pain or radiation makes ureteric stone less typical but bladder stone is possible.
supporting_evidence: Intermittent lower abdominal pain (comes and goes) rated 7/10
Dysuria can occur if stone irritates lower tract
opposing_evidence: No flank/loin pain or radiation to groin recorded (commonly seen with ureteric stones)
No history of renal colic episodes or stone disease
No imaging or urinalysis to confirm

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Would explain urinary symptoms plus hematuria but typically presents with systemic features (fever, rigors) and flank/loin pain which are absent here. Consider if symptoms worsen or fever develops.
supporting_evidence: Dysuria and hematuria can be present in ascending infections
opposing_evidence: No fever or feeling feverish reported
Patient clinically looks uncomplicated per history

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Visible hematuria is an alarm symptom for urothelial malignancy and should be considered, but bladder cancer is uncommon in younger patients without risk factors (eg heavy smoking, occupational exposures). Acute dysuria and malodour suggest infectious/inflammatory causes are more likely.
supporting_evidence: Visible hematuria (even spotting) — an indication to consider malignancy if persistent or unexplained
opposing_evidence: Age and lack of risk factors (non-smoker, no occupational exposure reported) make malignancy less likely
Acute onset with dysuria, malodour and suprapubic pain fits infection more than cancer
No weight loss or systemic features reported
